questions.prompt: In the sixth paragraph, what point does the writer make about the language used to teach in India's primary schools?
options: Contact with English outside the classroom is of little real use.
Being taught through English can put children from poor backgrounds at an even greater disadvantage.
Well-motivated children pick up English more readily than others.
Schools differ widely in the way they deliver English lessons.
questions.correct: Being taught through English can put children from poor backgrounds at an even greater disadvantage.

explanation.step1: In the sixth paragraph, what point does the writer make about the language used to teach in India's primary schools ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Tác giả nhận định gì về ngôn ngữ dùng để giảng dạy ở các trường tiểu học India?
explanation.step2: Đếm các đoạn nội dung và bỏ qua chú thích từ *slum* ở Đoạn 5: đoạn thứ sáu mà câu hỏi nhắc tới tương ứng với Đoạn 7 trên bài đọc. Bắt đầu đọc tại ý ngôn ngữ được chọn để giảng dạy (“the language chosen to teach in”). Đoạn 7 — the language chosen to teach in
explanation.step3: Đoạn 7: Early though the results still are, one thing has already emerged: the language chosen to teach in — English above all — can set back any child who arrives at school having barely met it , whether in the classroom or in the world beyond . On Halloran's reading, the weight of evidence , from her own work and from other studies, points to English-medium teaching being a poor fit for youngsters from the lowest income brackets , certainly for the opening three years of primary school . Câu (1): dùng English để giảng dạy có thể khiến trẻ chưa quen ngôn ngữ này gặp bất lợi . Câu (2): cách dạy đó không phù hợp với trẻ thuộc nhóm thu nhập thấp nhất . Dạy bằng English có thể khiến trẻ nghèo chịu thêm bất lợi , đặc biệt khi các em chưa quen ngôn ngữ này.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. Being taught through English can put children from poor backgrounds at an even greater disadvantage . ( Được dạy bằng English có thể khiến trẻ có hoàn cảnh nghèo khó chịu thêm bất lợi .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Being taught through English English medium teaching children from poor backgrounds youngsters from the lowest income brackets at an even greater disadvantage can set back + a poor fit Đáp án A “ Việc tiếp xúc với English ngoài lớp học hầu như không có ích ”: Nếu skim thấy cụm chỉ môi trường ngoài lớp học (“in the world beyond”), em có thể chọn nhầm Nhưng câu (1) nói thiếu tiếp xúc có thể gây bất lợi, không nói tiếp xúc bên ngoài là vô ích. Đáp án C “ Trẻ có động lực học English tiếp thu nhanh hơn trẻ khác ”: Sai vì bằng chứng nói về mức độ quen thuộc với ngôn ngữ giảng dạy, không nói đến động lực hay tốc độ học English. Đáp án D “ Các trường có cách dạy môn English rất khác nhau ”: Nếu skim Đoạn 6 thấy phương pháp trên lớp (“classroom methods teachers actually use”), em có thể chọn nhầm Nhưng câu (1)–(2) đoạn 7 bàn về dạy học bằng English, không phải các cách dạy môn English.

questions.prompt: What is Halloran implying when she uses the phrase 'that ship has sailed'?
options: Doing away with English as a teaching medium altogether is no longer a realistic option.
English teaching could be shaped more closely around what pupils actually need.
Efforts to teach English as a subject in its own right have mostly fallen short.
The study's conclusions will be of little use to certain pupils.
questions.correct: Doing away with English as a teaching medium altogether is no longer a realistic option.

explanation.step1: What is Halloran implying when she uses the phrase ' that ship has sailed ' ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Halloran ngụ ý điều gì khi nói “that ship has sailed”? Ta cần xác định thành ngữ này chỉ khả năng nào đã qua , không chỉ chọn một lời khuyên xuất hiện gần đó.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào cụm đặc biệt “that ship has sailed” => ta tìm đến lời Halloran ở đoạn 8. Đoạn 8 — that ship has sailed
explanation.step3: Đoạn 8: Nobody is proposing that English be dropped — that ship has sailed — the point is rather that we should pay closer heed to what learners require . Thành ngữ quay lại khả năng bỏ English (“English be dropped”): Halloran ngụ ý rằng việc ấy không còn là lựa chọn thực tế . Điều bà muốn nhấn mạnh *thay vào đó* là nhu cầu của người học.
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: A. Doing away with English as a teaching medium altogether is no longer a realistic option . (Loại bỏ hoàn toàn English khỏi vai trò ngôn ngữ giảng dạy không còn là lựa chọn thực tế.) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Doing away with English English be dropped no longer a realistic option that ship has sailed Lưu ý ý này không có nghĩa Halloran muốn tiếp tục dùng English làm ngôn ngữ giảng dạy ở tiểu học; bà phân biệt việc đó với chuyện loại bỏ English hoàn toàn. Đáp án B “ Việc dạy English có thể được điều chỉnh sát hơn với nhu cầu thực tế của học sinh ”: ngay sau thành ngữ có ý chú ý hơn đến nhu cầu người học (“pay closer heed to what learners require”). Nhưng đó là điều Halloran muốn làm thay thế, không phải hàm ý của thành ngữ. Đáp án C “ Những nỗ lực dạy English như một môn học riêng phần lớn đã thất bại ”: Đoạn 8 có nói đến việc dạy English như một môn riêng (“taught in its own right”), nhưng không nói cách dạy đó đã thất bại. Đáp án D “ Kết luận nghiên cứu sẽ ít có ích cho một số học sinh ”: Sai vì thành ngữ nói về khả năng bỏ English, không đánh giá kết luận nghiên cứu hữu ích đến đâu.

questions.prompt: In the eighth paragraph, which result is described as having taken the researchers by surprise?
options: Poor boys and girls turn out to have much the same level of general intelligence.
The age at which a child moves into a slum has no bearing on their results.
At reading and number work, slum children do no worse than other poor city children.
Slum children and other poor city children turn out to live much the same kind of life.
questions.correct: At reading and number work, slum children do no worse than other poor city children.

explanation.step1: In the eighth paragraph, which result is described as having taken the researchers by surprise ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Kết quả nào khiến nhóm nghiên cứu ngạc nhiên ? Ta cần phân biệt kết quả bất ngờ với những kết quả khác cũng được nêu trong đoạn.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh để tìm ý *gây ngạc nhiên*. Ở đoạn 9 của bản nguồn, cụm “a genuine surprise” => bắt đầu đọc tại đây. Đề gọi đây là đoạn thứ tám vì bản nguồn tách chú giải *slum* thành đoạn 5. Đoạn 9 — a genuine surprise
explanation.step3: Đoạn 9: The early data reveal no gap in general intelligence between boys and girls , nor between those from the slums and those from other hard-up city households — but a genuine surprise lay elsewhere . Far from trailing their peers from other poor urban homes, slum children keep pace with them and, on occasion, come out ahead, in numeracy and literacy exercises alike . Câu (1): Kết quả về trí thông minh được nêu trước, nhưng điều gây ngạc nhiên nằm ở kết quả khác . Câu (2): Trẻ ở khu ổ chuột không kém trẻ nghèo thành thị khác trong cả bài tính và đọc viết .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. At reading and number work , slum children do no worse than other poor city children . ( Trong bài đọc và bài tính , trẻ ở khu ổ chuột không kém trẻ nghèo thành thị khác .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: taken the researchers by surprise a genuine surprise do no worse than other poor city children Far from trailing their peers from other poor urban homes + keep pace with them At reading and number work in numeracy and literacy exercises alike Đáp án A “ Bé trai và bé gái nghèo có mức trí thông minh chung gần giống nhau ”: Nếu skim thấy “no gap in general intelligence” sẽ dễ chọn ý này Nhưng câu (1) nói điều gây ngạc nhiên nằm ở kết quả khác. Đáp án B “ Tuổi chuyển đến khu ổ chuột không ảnh hưởng đến kết quả của trẻ ”: Sai vì bằng chứng không xét tuổi chuyển đến khu ổ chuột. Đáp án D “ Trẻ ở khu ổ chuột và trẻ nghèo thành thị khác có lối sống gần giống nhau ”: Cụm “other poor urban homes” dễ khiến ta nghĩ đến đời sống của hai nhóm Nhưng câu (2) so sánh kết quả bài tập, không nói họ sống giống nhau.

passages.title: The Globemakers: The Curious Story of an Ancient Craft
passages.subtitle: (A review of Casimir Brandt's book The Globemakers)
content: A model globe for his mother's seventy-fifth birthday: that was all Casimir Brandt, then living in Edinburgh, set out to buy in 2010. Yet this modest idea, straightforward as it first appeared, grew into a near-obsession that consumed the best part of ten years and threw up enough setbacks to have discouraged a less stubborn person. By the time it was over, Brandt had founded what remains the only made-to-order globemaking firm in the world.

What The Globemakers, Brandt's record of this on-a-whim project, reveals first is that picking up such an object involved far more than clicking 'buy' online and wincing at the delivery charge. The notion that our forebears were hopelessly ignorant about geography is remarkably persistent, yet in truth the spherical shape of the Earth has been understood for more than two and a half thousand years. A stitched leather ball was the comparison drawn by the philosopher Demarchos in one of his surviving dialogues, and the earliest globe on record is generally credited to Straton of Assos, thought to have fashioned one somewhere around 160 BCE. A well-made globe, Brandt assumed, could hardly be hard to come by.

Roughly two thousand years on, though, the craft of making globes appeared to have slipped almost entirely out of memory. In the auction rooms Brandt found true antiques priced well beyond what he could afford, and elsewhere only crude mass-produced models meant for the schoolroom. Journeys as far afield as Turkey and Japan, where he had hoped the expertise of traditional cartographers* might have survived, led nowhere.

Undaunted, Brandt resolved to build a quality globe himself, whereupon virtually every step that could go wrong duly did. The Earth's form was a difficulty in itself: rather than a true sphere it is oblate, flattened a little at each pole. He settled on a compromise, two half-spheres joined together, but then could find nobody able to cast the moulds precisely enough to guarantee that the two halves would end up with matching circumferences. And once that had finally been sorted out, prising the pieces free of the moulds left the workshop behind his house strewn with broken plaster of Paris* and thick with a dust that caught in the throat.

* cartographer: someone involved in the science or practice of drawing maps * plaster of Paris: a quick-setting plaster consisting of a fine white powder that hardens when moistened and allowed to dry

What all these failed trials taught him about the difficulties of the craft, Brandt passes on to his readers. Working out how to ease the globes cleanly from their moulds — the answer, in the end, was a top-of-the-range air compressor — and tracking down paper and inks that would form the gores (the flat map segments glued onto the sphere) without the colour bleeding into an illegible smear, cost him many months and a startling sum of money. You can feel his exasperation as he describes the delicate business of fixing the gores in place, a stage reached only after he had hunted down a glue with exactly the right stickiness. And then, almost at the finish, came the discovery that the paper had stretched a fraction, leaving the last segment lapping over the first by a single centimetre — trivial-sounding, perhaps, until you realise that one centimetre stands for two per cent of the planet's diameter, enough to erase the Himalayas or rub out Chile.

Running alongside Brandt's account of these technical trials is a set of digressions on the master globemakers of earlier centuries and on the history of cartography more broadly. Those after fuller cartographic detail may feel a little short-changed, and yet in Joos van Dael the author plainly recognised a kindred spirit. It was van Dael, a craftsman of Bruges, who in 1489 produced the Wereldbol — the oldest globe still in existence — its surface exquisitely finished by a team of painters and other artisans, only for news to arrive that a westbound expedition had blundered upon unknown lands that very year, leaving his creation obsolete on the day it was done. A comparable, if still grander, single-mindedness marks the labours of the Venetian mapmaker Ludovico Farsetti, who in the eighteenth century built a pair of globes for an Austrian archduke. The colossal twins, each close to three and a half metres across, took him twenty-five years and survive today in the Imperial Library in Vienna.

For all that it celebrates the rebirth of an old craft, Brandt's book is at the same time an elegy for skills that are quietly disappearing. Setting out on his globemaking adventure, he found it hard to track down either artisans able to make the moulds correctly or foundries that could form the meridians — the metal hoops that encircle a globe — to the necessary standard. The right craftsmen did turn up in the end, a few of them simply wandering by chance into his workshop, which by then occupied rather better premises than his old back room, but a good number have since retired or died.

Brandt's mother did get her seventy-fifth birthday globe in the end, though a full two years behind schedule. Her son went on to establish a firm that today produces more than five hundred globes annually, making them for clients who might ask for their own small village to be marked or for stranger requests besides. Richly illustrated with photographs charting each phase of his undertaking, together with a handful of pictures of old globes and maps, the book is anything but a manual for turning a profit. What it does do, and amply, is kindle admiration — for the artistry of the great mapmakers of former times, and for the dogged obstinacy of the modern-day heir who brought their all-but-dead craft back to life.

questions.prompt: What Casimir Brandt had pictured as a simple present for his mother proved instead to be a surprisingly _____, one that obliged him to work through _____ before it was done. Acquiring the globe by means of an ordinary _____, he soon realised, was not going to be possible. The examples he did track down came in two kinds: _____ meant for _____, and costly antique pieces that lay well outside his budget. He even made trips to countries where the _____ for such work might still have survived, only to return without success.

explanation.step1: What Casimir Brandt had pictured as a simple present for his mother proved instead to be a surprisingly 1. ___ , Sau “a surprisingly”, cần một cụm kết thúc bằng danh từ số ít , gọi tên điều mà việc mua quà đã trở thành. “Instead” cho thấy thực tế trái với dự tính đơn giản ban đầu.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào chi tiết sinh nhật mẹ (“his mother's seventy-fifth birthday”) => ta bắt đầu đọc từ câu (1), đoạn 1. Đoạn 1
explanation.step3: Đoạn 1: A model globe for his mother's seventy-fifth birthday : that was all Casimir Brandt , then living in Edinburgh, set out to buy in 2010 . Yet this modest idea , straightforward as it first appeared , grew into a near-obsession that consumed the best part of ten years and threw up enough setbacks to have discouraged a less stubborn person . Câu (1): Casimir Brandt ban đầu chỉ định mua một quả địa cầu tặng mẹ. Câu (2): “Yet” đảo chiều dự tính ấy: việc tưởng đơn giản trở thành một công việc kéo dài, đòi hỏi nhiều công sức .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: demanding undertaking Câu hoàn chỉnh: What Casimir Brandt had pictured as a simple present for his mother proved instead to be a surprisingly demanding undertaking. (Điều Casimir Brandt tưởng là món quà đơn giản cho mẹ hóa ra lại là một công việc đòi hỏi nhiều công sức .) => Khớp với dự đoán về một công việc trái với dự tính ban đầu; bài đọc cho thấy nó cuốn Casimir Brandt vào gần mười năm. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: demanding undertaking grew into a near obsession + consumed the best part of ten years instead Yet treasured keepsake — kỷ vật quý giá: Quà sinh nhật dễ gợi đến một vật đáng trân trọng Nhưng chỗ trống gọi tên việc mua quà đã trở thành điều gì, không phải tên của món quà. persistent hurdles — những trở ngại dai dẳng: Từ “setbacks” ở câu (2) dễ gây nhầm Nhưng đây là các trở ngại trong quá trình thực hiện, lại là cụm số nhiều nên không thể đứng sau “a surprisingly”. internet order — đơn đặt hàng qua mạng: Đoạn 2 có ý mua hàng trực tuyến (“clicking 'buy' online”), nhưng ý định ấy không biến thành một đơn đặt hàng; nó trở thành một công việc đòi hỏi nhiều công sức.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 28 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: one that obliged him to work through 2. ___ before it was done . Chỗ trống đứng sau “work through”, nên cần một cụm danh từ chỉ những khó khăn phải vượt qua trước khi hoàn thành công việc.
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng Casimir Brandt => tìm đến đoạn 1, bắt đầu ở câu nói về món quà sinh nhật cho mẹ rồi đọc tiếp để xem dự định ấy diễn ra thế nào. Đoạn 1
explanation.step3: Đoạn 1: Yet this modest idea , straightforward as it first appeared, grew into a near-obsession that consumed the best part of ten years and threw up enough setbacks to have discouraged a less stubborn person .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: persistent hurdles Câu hoàn chỉnh: one that obliged him to work through persistent hurdles before it was done. (một công việc buộc Brandt vượt qua những trở ngại dai dẳng trước khi hoàn tất.) => Khớp với dự đoán về những khó khăn phải vượt qua: bài đọc nói đến nhiều trở ngại (“enough setbacks”) trong một việc ngốn gần mười năm (“consumed the best part of ten years”). Đối chiếu paraphrasing: hurdles setbacks persistent consumed the best part of ten years demanding undertaking — công việc đòi hỏi nhiều công sức: Sai vì cụm này mô tả cả công việc, không phải những trở ngại đứng sau “work through”; đây cũng là ý của chỗ trống 1. unusual materials — vật liệu khác thường: Nếu đọc lướt đoạn 6, em có thể bị hút vào chi tiết giấy và mực (“paper and inks”) Nhưng vật liệu không phải những trở ngại (“setbacks”) được hỏi ở đây. specialist know-how — chuyên môn đặc thù: Đoạn 3 có nhắc đến chuyên môn của người làm bản đồ (“expertise of traditional cartographers”), nhưng đó không phải những trở ngại Brandt phải vượt qua.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 29 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: Acquiring the globe by means of an ordinary 3. ___ , he soon realised, was not going to be possible . Ô trống đứng sau “an ordinary”, nên cần một cụm danh từ số ít chỉ cách thức mua quả địa cầu. Câu hỏi nói cách đó không khả thi .
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng Casimir Brandt và ý tìm mua quả địa cầu => ta bắt đầu đọc câu (1) đoạn 2, tại cụm “picking up such an object”. Đoạn 2 — picking up such an object
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: What The Globemakers , Brandt's record of this on-a-whim project, reveals first is that picking up such an object involved far more than clicking 'buy' online and wincing at the delivery charge . Việc có được quả địa cầu đòi hỏi nhiều hơn thao tác nhấn mua trên mạng. Vậy cách mua thông thường được nhắc đến là đặt hàng qua mạng .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: internet order Câu hoàn chỉnh: Acquiring the globe by means of an ordinary internet order , he soon realised, was not going to be possible. (Brandt sớm nhận ra rằng không thể có được quả địa cầu chỉ bằng một đơn đặt hàng qua mạng thông thường .) => Khớp với dự đoán về một cách mua thông thường: bài đọc cho thấy chỉ nhấn mua trực tuyến là không đủ . Đối chiếu paraphrasing: internet order clicking 'buy' online not going to be possible involved far more than việc nhấn mua trực tuyến returns policy — chính sách trả hàng: Dễ nhầm vì cũng liên quan đến mua hàng, nhưng đây là quy định sau khi mua, không phải cách có được quả địa cầu. specialist know-how — kiến thức chuyên môn: Bài đọc có nói đến chuyên môn làm địa cầu ở đoạn 3, nhưng ô trống này hỏi về cách đặt mua, không phải kỹ năng chế tác. overseas buyers — người mua ở nước ngoài: Có từ liên quan đến việc mua, nhưng đây là người mua, không phải cách mua; dạng số nhiều cũng không đi sau “an ordinary”.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 30 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: The examples he did track down came in two kinds : 4. ___ meant for 5. ___ , and costly antique pieces that lay well outside his budget . Chỗ trống 4 cần một cụm danh từ số nhiều chỉ một loại địa cầu . Vì loại còn lại là đồ cổ đắt tiền, ta dự đoán cần tìm những mẫu địa cầu có chất lượng thấp .
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng Brandt và ý tìm được hai loại địa cầu, ta đến đoạn 3 và bắt đầu đọc câu (2). Đoạn 3
explanation.step3: Đoạn 3: In the auction rooms Brandt found true antiques priced well beyond what he could afford , and elsewhere only crude mass-produced models meant for the schoolroom . Brandt tìm thấy đồ cổ quá đắt; ở nơi khác, ông chỉ tìm được những mẫu địa cầu thô sơ . Đây là loại cần điền ở chỗ trống 4.
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: low-grade versions Câu hoàn chỉnh: The examples he did track down came in two kinds: low-grade versions meant for 5. ___, and costly antique pieces that lay well outside his budget. (Những mẫu ông tìm được thuộc hai loại: các phiên bản chất lượng thấp dành cho mục đích ở chỗ trống 5, và những món đồ cổ đắt tiền vượt quá ngân sách của ông.) => Khớp với dự đoán về mẫu địa cầu chất lượng thấp và cách bài đọc mô tả chúng. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: low grade versions crude + models classroom use “ việc sử dụng trong lớp học ”: bài đọc có cụm chỉ mục đích sử dụng (“meant for the schoolroom”). Nhưng chỗ trống 4 hỏi loại mẫu địa cầu, còn mục đích sử dụng thuộc chỗ trống 5. unusual materials “ vật liệu khác thường ”: Sai vì bài đọc nói đến những mẫu địa cầu (“models”), không phải vật liệu làm ra chúng.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 31 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: 4. ___ meant for 5. ___ Sau “meant for”, cần một cụm danh từ chỉ mục đích sử dụng của loại địa cầu ở chỗ trống 4.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến khi gặp ý nói địa cầu được làm để dùng vào việc gì. Cụm “meant for the schoolroom” ở đoạn 3 cho biết đây là vùng liên quan. Đoạn 3 — meant for the schoolroom
explanation.step3: Đoạn 3: In the auction rooms Brandt found true antiques priced well beyond what he could afford , and elsewhere only crude mass-produced models meant for the schoolroom .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: classroom use Câu hoàn chỉnh: The examples he did track down came in two kinds: 4. ___ meant for classroom use, and costly antique pieces that lay well outside his budget. (Những thứ Brandt tìm được gồm hai loại: 4. ___ dành để sử dụng trong lớp học và những món đồ cổ đắt tiền vượt quá ngân sách của anh.) => Khớp với dự đoán: đây là mục đích sử dụng , vì các mẫu địa cầu được làm cho phòng học. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: the schoolroom classroom use low-grade versions “ — những mẫu chất lượng thấp ”: câu bằng chứng có “crude mass-produced models”. Nhưng cụm này chỉ loại địa cầu ở chỗ trống 4, không phải mục đích sử dụng ở chỗ trống 5. overseas buyers “ — người mua ở nước ngoài ”: Cụm này có thể đứng sau “meant for” về ngữ pháp, nhưng bài đọc nói “the schoolroom”, không nói đến người mua. treasured keepsake “ — kỷ vật quý giá ”: Món quà sinh nhật có thể gợi liên tưởng đến kỷ vật Nhưng những mẫu địa cầu trong câu bằng chứng được làm cho phòng học.

questions.prompt: Complete blank 32 using words from the box:

explanation.step1: He even made trips to countries where the 6. ___ for such work might still have survived , only to return without success . Chỗ trống cần một cụm danh từ sau “the”. Ta dự đoán đó là một loại kiến thức hoặc kỹ năng phục vụ công việc này, có thể vẫn còn ở những nơi Brandt đến tìm.
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta tìm ý đi đến các nước (“trips to countries”). Ở đoạn 3, cụm những chuyến đi xa (“Journeys as far afield as Turkey and Japan”) => đây là vùng cần đọc. Đoạn 3 — Journeys as far afield as Turkey and Japan
explanation.step3: Đoạn 3: Journeys as far afield as Turkey and Japan , where he had hoped the expertise of traditional cartographers* might have survived , led nowhere .
explanation.step4: Đáp án phù hợp nhất: specialist know-how Câu hoàn chỉnh: He even made trips to countries where the specialist know-how for such work might still have survived, only to return without success. (Brandt thậm chí đến những nước mà kiến thức chuyên môn cho công việc này có thể vẫn còn, nhưng cuối cùng không tìm được gì.) => Khớp với dự đoán: thứ Brandt tìm là chuyên môn , được bài đọc gọi là “expertise”. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: expertise specialist know how led nowhere return without success unusual materials — vật liệu khác thường: Việc làm địa cầu có thể khiến em nghĩ đến vật liệu, nhưng câu (3) nói về chuyên môn (“expertise”), không phải vật liệu. overseas buyers — người mua ở nước ngoài: Turkey và Japan là nơi Brandt đến tìm chuyên môn, không phải nơi ông tìm người mua. persistent hurdles — những trở ngại dai dẳng: Chuyến đi không thành công (“led nowhere”) dễ gợi ý khó khăn, nhưng thứ có thể còn tồn tại (“might have survived”) là chuyên môn, không phải trở ngại.

questions.prompt: The writer rejects the idea that people long ago had little understanding of geography.

explanation.step1: The writer rejects the idea that people long ago had little understanding of geography . Ý câu hỏi: Người viết có bác bỏ quan niệm người thời xưa biết rất ít về địa lý không?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc đến khi gặp ý *người xưa thiếu hiểu biết về địa lý*. Ở đoạn 2, cụm “our forebears were hopelessly ignorant about geography” là điểm bắt đầu đọc. Đoạn 2 — our forebears were hopelessly ignorant about geography
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: The notion that our forebears were hopelessly ignorant about geography is remarkably persistent , yet in truth the spherical shape of the Earth has been understood for more than two and a half thousand years .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: người viết bác bỏ (“rejects”) quan niệm người thời xưa biết rất ít về địa lý. Bài đọc nói: quan niệm ấy vẫn tồn tại, nhưng thực ra (“yet in truth”), người ta đã hiểu Earth có dạng cầu từ hơn hai nghìn năm trước. Đây là lập trường trái với quan niệm ấy . Đối chiếu paraphrasing: people long ago our forebears little understanding of geography hopelessly ignorant about geography rejects yet in truth Đáp án đúng: YES Đáp án NO Nếu chỉ thấy quan niệm ấy vẫn tồn tại (“is remarkably persistent”), ta dễ tưởng người viết đồng tình Nhưng “yet in truth” dẫn sang điều người viết cho là đúng và trái với quan niệm ấy. Chỉ chọn NO nếu người viết khẳng định người xưa thực sự thiếu hiểu biết về địa lý. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ tìm đúng từ “rejects”, ta có thể tưởng bài không cho biết lập trường Nhưng “yet in truth” đã thể hiện sự bác bỏ. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu bài không cho thấy người viết tán thành hay bác bỏ quan niệm đó.

questions.prompt: The first globe that we know of is attributed to Demarchos.

explanation.step1: The first globe that we know of is attributed to Demarchos . Ý câu hỏi: tác giả có ghi nhận Demarchos là người làm ra quả địa cầu đầu tiên được biết đến không?
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng Demarchos => ta tìm đến câu (3) ở đoạn 2, nơi tác giả nhắc đến ông. Đoạn 2
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: A stitched leather ball was the comparison drawn by the philosopher Demarchos in one of his surviving dialogues , and the earliest globe on record is generally credited to Straton of Assos , thought to have fashioned one somewhere around 160 BCE .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: quả địa cầu đầu tiên được ghi nhận là của Demarchos (“attributed to Demarchos”). Bài đọc nói: Demarchos đưa ra một phép so sánh; quả địa cầu sớm nhất được ghi nhận là của Straton of Assos (“is generally credited to Straton of Assos ”). Người được ghi nhận khác nhau => khẳng định trái với điều tác giả viết. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: first globe that we know of the earliest globe on record attributed to Demarchos credited to Straton of Assos Đáp án đúng: NO Đáp án YES Nếu skim/scan thấy tên Demarchos trong câu (3), sẽ dễ chọn YES Nhưng tác giả gắn ông với phép so sánh, không phải quả địa cầu đầu tiên. Chỉ chọn YES nếu tác giả ghi nhận quả địa cầu đó là của Demarchos. NOT GIVEN Sai vì tác giả nêu rõ người được ghi nhận là Straton of Assos. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu tác giả không cho biết quả địa cầu đầu tiên được ghi nhận là của ai.

questions.prompt: Straton is thought to have created his globe as a teaching aid.

explanation.step1: Straton is thought to have created his globe as a teaching aid . Ý câu hỏi: tác giả có nói quả địa cầu của Straton được tạo ra để dạy học hay không?
explanation.step2: Dựa vào tên riêng `Straton` => ta định vị được câu (3) ở đoạn 2. Đoạn 2
explanation.step3: Đoạn 2: A stitched leather ball was the comparison drawn by the philosopher Demarchos in one of his surviving dialogues , and the earliest globe on record is generally credited to Straton of Assos , thought to have fashioned one somewhere around 160 BCE .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Straton tạo quả địa cầu để dạy học (“ as a teaching aid ”). Bài đọc nói: quả địa cầu sớm nhất được ghi nhận được quy cho Straton (“is generally credited to Straton”), nhưng không nói ông tạo nó để làm gì . Đối chiếu paraphrasing: is thought to have created is generally credited to Straton as a teaching aid không có trong bài Đáp án đúng: NOT GIVEN Đáp án YES Nếu skim/scan thấy đoạn 3 nói các quả địa cầu dùng trong trường học (“meant for the schoolroom”), sẽ dễ chọn YES Nhưng đó là các mẫu sản xuất hàng loạt Brandt tìm thấy, không phải quả địa cầu của Straton. Chỉ chọn YES nếu tác giả nói Straton tạo quả địa cầu để dạy học. Đáp án NO Sai vì tác giả không nêu mục đích, chứ không phủ nhận mục đích dạy học. Chỉ chọn NO nếu tác giả nói Straton không tạo quả địa cầu để dạy học, hoặc nêu một mục đích loại trừ việc đó.

questions.prompt: Brandt eventually located a suitable globe while travelling abroad.

explanation.step1: Brandt eventually located a suitable globe while travelling abroad . Ý câu hỏi: tác giả có nói Brandt đã tìm được một quả địa cầu phù hợp trong chuyến đi nước ngoài không?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta tìm ý đi nước ngoài và gặp những chuyến đi xa tới Turkey (“Journeys as far afield as Turkey”) ở đoạn 3 => đây là vùng cần đọc. Đoạn 3 — Journeys as far afield as Turkey
explanation.step3: Đoạn 3: Journeys as far afield as Turkey and Japan , where he had hoped the expertise of traditional cartographers* might have survived, led nowhere .
explanation.step4: Câu hỏi nói: Brandt tìm được địa cầu phù hợp (“located a suitable globe”) khi đi nước ngoài . Bài đọc nói: các chuyến đi xa của ông không đem lại kết quả (“led no where”). Đây là kết quả trái với điều statement khẳng định , nên lập trường của tác giả là NO , không phải NOT GIVEN. Đối chiếu paraphrasing: while travelling abroad Journeys as far afield as Turkey eventually located a suitable globe led nowhere Đáp án đúng: NO Đáp án YES Nếu chỉ thấy chuyến đi xa tới Turkey, ta có thể tưởng Brandt đã tìm được thứ cần mua Nhưng tác giả nói các chuyến đi không đem lại kết quả (“led nowhere”). Chỉ chọn YES nếu tác giả nói Brandt tìm được địa cầu phù hợp trong chuyến đi. NOT GIVEN Nếu chỉ đọc địa điểm mà bỏ qua kết quả, ta có thể tưởng bài không cho biết chuyến đi thành công hay không Nhưng “led nowhere” đã nêu rõ kết quả. Chỉ chọn NOT GIVEN nếu tác giả không cho biết kết quả của những chuyến đi đó.

questions.prompt: When Brandt came to fix the gores onto the surface of the globe,
options: he realised that speed was essential.
he began to doubt the quality of his materials.
a problem he had not foreseen came to light.
he came close to abandoning the whole project.
questions.correct: a problem he had not foreseen came to light.

explanation.step1: When Brandt came to fix the gores onto the surface of the globe , Câu hỏi hỏi: Khi Brandt gắn các mảnh bản đồ lên bề mặt quả địa cầu, chuyện gì đã xảy ra?
explanation.step2: Dựa vào từ khoá đặc biệt gores => ta định vị được câu (3), đoạn 6, ở cụm chỉ việc gắn các mảnh bản đồ (“fixing the gores in place”). Đoạn 6
explanation.step3: Đoạn 6: You can feel his exasperation as he describes the delicate business of fixing the gores in place , a stage reached only after he had hunted down a glue with exactly the right stickiness . And then , almost at the finish, came the discovery that the paper had stretched a fraction , leaving the last segment lapping over the first by a single centimetre — trivial-sounding, perhaps, until you realise that one centimetre stands for two per cent of the planet's diameter, enough to erase the Himalayas or rub out Chile . Câu (3): xác định công đoạn gắn gores; Brandt thấy công đoạn này gây bực bội. Câu (4): tiếp đó, ông phát hiện giấy giãn khiến mảnh cuối chồng lên mảnh đầu .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. a problem he had not foreseen came to light . (Một sự cố ông không lường trước đã lộ ra.) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: came to light came the discovery a problem he had not foreseen the paper had stretched a fraction + the last segment lapping over the first Đáp án A “ Ông nhận ra tốc độ là yếu tố thiết yếu ”: Sai vì phát hiện ở câu (4) liên quan đến giấy bị giãn, không phải tốc độ thực hiện. Đáp án B “ Ông bắt đầu nghi ngờ chất lượng vật liệu ”: Nếu skim thấy giấy bị giãn (“the paper had stretched a fraction”), ta dễ nghĩ giấy kém chất lượng Nhưng bài chỉ nói sự cố xảy ra, không nói Brandt bắt đầu nghi ngờ vật liệu. Đáp án D “ Ông suýt từ bỏ toàn bộ dự án ”: Sự bực bội (“his exasperation”) dễ gây nhầm lẫn, nhưng bực bội không đồng nghĩa với suýt bỏ cuộc.

questions.prompt: The reviewer brings in globemakers of earlier times mainly to show that
options: their accomplishments deserve to be far better known.
Brandt resembled each of them in some way.
Brandt drew particular inspiration from them.
their struggles need not have happened at all.
questions.correct: Brandt resembled each of them in some way.

explanation.step1: The reviewer brings in globemakers of earlier times mainly to show that Câu hỏi hỏi: Người viết nhắc đến những người làm quả địa cầu thời trước chủ yếu để làm rõ điều gì?
explanation.step2: Câu hỏi không có từ khoá đặc biệt; ta đọc nhanh đến cụm chỉ những người làm quả địa cầu ở các thế kỷ trước (“master globemakers of earlier centuries”) trong đoạn 7 => đây là điểm bắt đầu tìm mục đích người viết nhắc đến họ. Đoạn 7 — master globemakers of earlier centuries
explanation.step3: Đoạn 7: Those after fuller cartographic detail may feel a little short-changed , and yet in Joos van Dael the author plainly recognised a kindred spirit . It was van Dael , a craftsman of Bruges, who in 1489 produced the Wereldbol — the oldest globe still in existence — its surface exquisitely finished by a team of painters and other artisans , only for news to arrive that a westbound expedition had blundered upon unknown lands that very year , leaving his creation obsolete on the day it was done . A comparable , if still grander, single-mindedness marks the labours of the Venetian mapmaker Ludovico Farsetti , who in the eighteenth century built a pair of globes for an Austrian archduke . Câu (2)–(3): Brandt xem Joos van Dael là người đồng điệu ; câu sau kể về công trình của van Dael. Câu (4): Ludovico Farsetti cũng được gắn với sự kiên tâm tương tự . Hai người làm quả địa cầu thời trước được nhắc đến để làm nổi bật nét tương đồng với Brandt .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. Brandt resembled each of them in some way . (Brandt có điểm giống với từng người trong số họ.) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: Brandt resembled each of them in some way a kindred spirit (Joos van Dael) + comparable single mindedness (Ludovico Farsetti). Đáp án A “ Thành tựu của họ đáng được biết đến rộng rãi hơn nhiều ”: Đoạn 9 ca ngợi nghệ thuật của các nhà vẽ bản đồ xưa (“artistry of the great mapmakers”), nhưng không nói thành tựu của họ chưa được biết đến đủ rộng. Đáp án C “ Brandt lấy cảm hứng đặc biệt từ họ ”: Dễ nhầm việc Brandt nhận ra một người đồng điệu (“a kindred spirit”) với việc lấy người ấy làm nguồn cảm hứng. Bài chỉ nêu sự giống nhau. Đáp án D “ Những trắc trở của họ hoàn toàn có thể tránh được ”: Việc tác phẩm của van Dael trở nên lỗi thời (“obsolete”) là một kết cục đáng tiếc, nhưng bài không nói những trắc trở ấy có thể tránh được.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make about Brandt in the seventh paragraph?
options: He places a high value on careful planning.
He laments how much traditional expertise is being lost.
He kept up lasting relationships with many craftsmen.
He understands why traditional crafts attract so little interest.
questions.correct: He laments how much traditional expertise is being lost.

explanation.step1: What point does the writer make about Brandt in the seventh paragraph ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Người viết nhận xét gì về Brandt trong đoạn văn thứ bảy?
explanation.step2: Đoạn văn xuôi thứ bảy tương ứng với Đoạn 8 của bản in này, vì Đoạn 5 chỉ là chú giải từ vựng. Bắt đầu đọc từ câu mở đầu “For all that it celebrates”. Đoạn 8 — For all that it celebrates
explanation.step3: Đoạn 8: For all that it celebrates the rebirth of an old craft , Brandt's book is at the same time an elegy for skills that are quietly disappearing . Qua cuốn sách, Brandt tiếc nuối những kỹ năng truyền thống đang mất đi , dù nghề cũ đang được khôi phục.
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: B. He laments how much traditional expertise is being lost . (Ông tiếc nuối việc nhiều kỹ năng truyền thống đang mai một .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: an elegy laments skills that are quietly disappearing traditional expertise is being lost Đáp án A “ Ông rất coi trọng việc lên kế hoạch cẩn thận ”: Sai vì câu (1) nói về sự mai một kỹ năng, không đánh giá cách Brandt lập kế hoạch. Đáp án C “ Ông duy trì quan hệ lâu dài với nhiều thợ thủ công ”: Đoạn 8 có nói ông tìm được thợ (“right craftsmen did turn up”), nhưng điều đó không chứng minh họ duy trì quan hệ lâu dài. Đáp án D “ Ông hiểu vì sao nghề thủ công truyền thống ít được quan tâm ”: Việc các kỹ năng đang biến mất không có nghĩa bài đọc giải thích nguyên nhân là nghề ít được quan tâm.

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph, what does the reviewer say about Brandt's book?
options: It gives too little detail about individual customers.
It offers no guidance on running a money-making enterprise.
It says nothing about where globe-making is heading.
questions.correct: It offers no guidance on running a money-making enterprise.

explanation.step1: In the final paragraph , what does the reviewer say about Brandt's book ? Câu hỏi hỏi: Ở đoạn cuối, người viết bài điểm sách nhận xét gì về cuốn sách của Brandt?
explanation.step2: Đoạn cuối là đoạn 9. Ta tìm chỗ người viết trực tiếp nhận xét về cuốn sách (“the book”). Đoạn 9 — the book
explanation.step3: Đoạn 9: Richly illustrated with photographs charting each phase of his undertaking, together with a handful of pictures of old globes and maps, the book is anything but a manual for turning a profit .
explanation.step4: Đáp án đúng: C. It offers no guidance on running a money-making enterprise . (Cuốn sách không hướng dẫn cách điều hành doanh nghiệp kiếm lời .) Đối chiếu paraphrasing: offers no guidance anything but a manual running a money making enterprise turning a profit Đáp án A “ Sách cung cấp quá ít chi tiết về từng khách hàng ”: Đoạn 9 có nhắc đến khách hàng (“clients who might ask”), nhưng đó là khách hàng của công ty; người viết không nhận xét rằng sách thiếu chi tiết về họ. Đáp án B “ Sách bỏ sót một số nhà làm bản đồ quan trọng ”: Cụm “great mapmakers of former times” dễ khiến ta nghĩ đến nội dung này, nhưng người viết bày tỏ sự ngưỡng mộ dành cho họ, không nói sách bỏ sót họ. Đáp án D “ Sách không nói gì về tương lai nghề làm địa cầu ”: Đoạn 8 có nói các kỹ năng đang dần biến mất (“quietly disappearing”), nhưng không khẳng định sách không bàn về tương lai nghề này.

passages.title: Oyster Bay Sailing Club Courses
content: 📌 General information

Participants need to be competent swimmers.Bring appropriate clothes, a [ _____ ] and personal toiletries such as shampoo.Food and snacks can be bought from the club’s [ _____ ].Learners are advised to watch online training [ _____ ] before attending.Secure [ _____ ] can be used by people taking the course.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking a sailing club representative about beginner courses. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:49] WOMAN: Good morning Oyster Bay Sailing Club. What can I do for you?
[00:53] MAN: Hi, I'm calling to ask about courses for someone who's new to sailing.
[00:58] WOMAN: Certainly, are you looking for yourself?
[01:00] MAN: Yes. I've read the information on your website, but I still can't work out which course would suit me best.
[01:08] WOMAN: Right. One possibility is one of our taster days.
[01:13] MAN: That might work.
[01:14] WOMAN: They're intended for complete beginners. The day gives you a first experience of sailing, so you can decide whether it's something you'd like to continue with.
[01:25] MAN: What does a day cost?
[01:27] WOMAN: A single booking is £120. If two people book together, the price falls to £110 per person.
[01:37] MAN: It'll only be me.
[01:39] WOMAN: That's no problem. The groups are kept quite small. We normally have around eight learners and ten is the absolute maximum. People tend to be very welcoming as well.
[01:52] MAN: OK. Is there another course that could be suitable?
[01:55] WOMAN: Yes. The alternative is level one. Hmm. Let's see.
[02:01] WOMAN: It runs over a weekend for two days and we offer it throughout the year.
[02:07] MAN: And what does that course cover?

[02:09] WOMAN: Well, there's both classroom work and practical training. The theory includes weather conditions, which you obviously need to understand, along with the tides. You'll also develop the basic skills needed to handle a boat. For the practical sessions, you go into the harbour in dinghies designed for beginners.
[02:32] WOMAN: There are two learners in each boat with an instructor who makes sure everyone receives all the necessary safety guidance.
[02:40] MAN: That sounds fairly demanding.
[02:42] WOMAN: It is quite intensive, but it's enjoyable too.
[02:46] MAN: How much is level one?
[02:48] WOMAN: The fee is £200. Members pay a little less though. The club offers them a discount, you see.
[02:55] MAN: That's nice. Um, well, I haven't decided whether to become a member though.
[03:03] WOMAN: There's no need to decide straight away.
[03:05] MAN: Is everything covered by that fee?

[03:08] WOMAN: Yes, it's all included. We also give you a very handy dictionary of sailing terms. Beginners often find the vocabulary difficult at first and the illustrations in it make the explanations much clearer. Once you finish the course, you're awarded a certificate.
[03:28] WOMAN: After that, you can progress to level two.
[03:31] MAN: Oh, okay. That sounds good.
[03:39] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen carefully and answer questions seven to ten.
[04:25] WOMAN: That covers the courses. There are just a few practical points you should know. First, everyone taking part needs to be able to swim.
[04:35] MAN: That's fine. I'm comfortable in the water.
[04:39] WOMAN: Good. We supply wetsuits and life jackets, but you'll need your own swimming trunks and an old pair of trainers.
[04:46] MAN: Should I bring a towel as well?
[04:49] WOMAN: Yes, definitely. You may also want your own toiletries, such as shampoo.
[04:53] MAN: What happens about meals? Do I need to bring something or does the club have a cafe?
[05:00] WOMAN: There's a cafe on site. It sells sandwiches, cakes and snacks, and the prices are quite reasonable.
[05:07] MAN: Great. I'm leaning towards level one, but I have no experience at all. Is there anything I could do beforehand?
[05:16] WOMAN: I'd suggest watching the videos we use as training material. They're online and I can email you the link. They'll help you understand what the course will be like.
[05:27] MAN: Excellent. Thank you. One last question. I'll probably come by bicycle, so I'll need a secure place for my valuables.

passages.title: Working as a makeup trainee
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Working as a makeup trainee"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a podcast host introducing a film makeup artist who explains what trainees can expect from the job. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Hello, and welcome back to our filmmaking podcast.

[00:54] AUDIO: This week, Claire Lamar is here to explain how people can begin a career as a makeup artist. Claire has worked in film makeup for more than 20 years, so she has plenty of practical advice for anyone hoping to enter the industry. Thanks, Ian. Before you can work as a film makeup artist, you'll normally spend roughly two years as a trainee.

[01:17] AUDIO: A low-budget short film is often a sensible place to find your first position. You shouldn't expect a salary on a production like that because the work is usually unpaid. Even so, the experience can make it worthwhile. You should insist that the cost of getting to and from the location is paid.

[01:39] AUDIO: Food, on the other hand, is rarely supplied, so make sure you take enough with you. You may be fortunate enough to begin on a film with a much larger budget, and that can provide especially valuable experience. Hair and makeup are handled by separate teams on productions of that size, so no one will expect you to style elaborate curls. You will, however, probably work with performers of many ages and from a variety of ethnic backgrounds.

[02:13] AUDIO: Special effects makeup requires expert training, so a beginner is unlikely to be allowed to practice it. Something trainees often find challenging is the pressure in a makeup department. There's almost always another task to do, so long periods of sitting around are unusual. The work can certainly be stressful.

[02:35] AUDIO: Experienced makeup artists remain professional even when a director is impatient or criticises what they've done. Watch how your supervisor responds and keep your own manner calm. Over the years, I've met a great many well-known actors. The first few times, I was completely overwhelmed.

[02:57] AUDIO: I admired them so much that I could barely say anything. That's still better than becoming overexcited and asking them to pose for photographs with you. These days, meeting the cast simply feels like a routine part of work. In fact, without their screen makeup, many actors look perfectly ordinary.

[03:20] AUDIO: Every trainee needs a makeup kit and should have it available wherever they're working. For the basic jobs trainees are given, a small collection of essential items is enough. You don't need anything sophisticated. It's useful to notice what more experienced artists keep in their own kits.

[03:42] AUDIO: Just remember that you must never take one of their products without first asking. You also need to develop a portfolio. Photograph every piece of work you complete and, when possible, record several stages as the makeup is being applied. Before using any of those images though, you must obtain permission from the makeup designer who leads the department.

[04:08] AUDIO: Your portfolio will normally be sent electronically, so there is no reason to produce printed copies. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. So, what duties does a makeup trainee carry out?

[05:04] AUDIO: It's worth considering whether the work suits your personality and whether you'd actually enjoy the routine. Let me describe some typical responsibilities. One possible job is preparing an actor before the makeup artist begins. Some performers arrive after already cleaning and moisturising their skin.

[05:25] AUDIO: If they haven't, you may need to do it for them and you must finish promptly. Any delay could put the makeup artist behind the production timetable. Trainees also contribute to continuity. You'll take photographs, enter them into the electronic record, and make a paper copy for the individual performer's file.

[05:48] AUDIO: All of this material has to be arranged carefully. If a scene is filmed again several months later, the team may need to reproduce the original makeup exactly. Then there are general duties. These could involve making tea and coffee one minute and putting a load of washing on the next.

[06:07] AUDIO: A cheerful approach and a readiness to take on whatever task is needed will improve your chances of being hired for another film. You won't put makeup on the leading cast, but you may be allowed to work on background performers. When a scene includes dozens of them, you have to move at a fast rate and avoid spending too much time on any one person. Doing that successfully also requires a fair amount of self-confidence.
[06:37] AUDIO: Now, let's turn to employment terms and working conditions. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Lecture on ocean biodiversity
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Lecture on ocean biodiversity"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a lecture and several resources about ocean biodiversity. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:49] PHIL: The talk by yesterday's visiting lecturer was worthwhile, wasn't it?

[00:53] LUCY: Definitely. I found out a great deal about biodiversity in the oceans. I'd already read around the subject and last year I wrote an assignment on some related problems. What I particularly appreciated, though, was her emphasis on threats that may develop over the longer term.

[01:10] PHIL: Yes, she covered matters that received very little public attention at present, but could become extremely significant in future. That made a strong impression on me as well. The ending wasn't especially optimistic, since many of those difficulties don't seem to have a straightforward answer.
[01:25] LUCY: True, although she did identify areas where changes in policy might help safeguard marine habitats and coastlines.

[01:33] PHIL: Hmm, but those proposals only concerned action within individual countries. Her illustrations came from across the world, and that global perspective showed me how extensive the dangers to ocean biodiversity really are.
[01:47] LUCY: I felt the same.
[01:48] PHIL: The research program she described sounded remarkable too. It can't be common to bring such a large number of experts into one project.

[01:57] LUCY: And their areas of expertise were so varied. It must have been a fascinating group to join. I recognized the names of two researchers who had taken part in earlier work, warning about pollution in the oceans.
[02:11] PHIL: That issue is much more widely recognized now, though, isn't it?
[02:15] LUCY: I'd say so.
[02:16] PHIL: The researchers were also based in countries all over the world. Still, international teams are probably less unusual these days because people can collaborate online.
[02:26] LUCY: Right. I was glad she didn't overwhelm us with statistics. The figures were available, but she concentrated on the broader conclusions that could be drawn from them.
[02:37] PHIL: Hmm. I was especially interested in the advances in equipment for monitoring sea creatures, as well as the robots she mentioned.
[02:45] LUCY: Yes, particularly her explanation of how robotic devices can help scientists examine risks to biodiversity.
[02:58] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:41] PHIL: Since we're both here, shall we go through the resources we need to assess for tomorrow's seminar? I've reviewed all of them, although I had to do it rather quickly.
[03:49] LUCY: Sure. What was your view of the article about invasive lionfish, the one arguing that their range was spreading across the Mediterranean?

[03:59] PHIL: The author repeatedly described the serious environmental harm they might cause, and that may well be accurate. The trouble was that there was hardly any supporting material showing why we should accept the claim.
[04:11] LUCY: Yes, I noticed that, too.
[04:13] PHIL: I also put on the documentary about microplastics. I only watched the beginning because I discovered it had been produced a decade earlier and decided not to continue.
[04:24] LUCY: I finished it, but I agree that its age was obvious. At the time it was made, hardly anyone knew about microplastics. Now the subject and its risks are familiar to almost everybody.
[04:37] PHIL: Exactly. What about the podcast dealing with pollution in the oceans?
[04:42] LUCY: I listened to it, but I learned nothing from it. Nearly everything the presenter said was completely expected.

[04:50] PHIL: I had the same reaction. It listed pesticides, plastic, and similar pollutants, then simply said they were harmful. That is new information for anyone. Did you manage the book about coastal ecosystems?

[05:04] LUCY: The one written by John Harper? Yes. Initially I found the level of detail difficult, especially the sections on offshore wind farms and fish farming. By the end, though, I understood the main problems far more clearly.
[05:20] PHIL: So did I. It summarized those issues very effectively, and the diagrams made the explanations easier to follow.

[05:27] LUCY: I couldn't cope with the article about metal toxicity. The discussion of metals from industrial emissions reacting in seawater was much too advanced for me, and I'm still confused by it.
[05:39] PHIL: I stopped after the opening section because I simply couldn't follow the argument.
[05:43] LUCY: The podcast about floating cities at sea was engaging, but I thought it gave only one side of the case.
[05:51] PHIL: Yes. It concentrated on the advantages for people and left out the possible environmental consequences.
[05:58] LUCY: Anyway, shall we decide how to present our evaluation?
[06:05] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 Sources of rubber
Three materials on which an industrial society depends
[ _____ ]fossil fuelsrubber
Natural rubber
Most is obtained from the Pará rubber tree, which is now grown in South-East Asia.
Availability is restricted because:

the tree’s development is [ _____ ].producers cannot respond rapidly to changing [ _____ ].plantations are limited to areas close to the [ _____ ].collecting latex requires a large workforce.used rubber is extremely hard to [ _____ ].
More recent dangers include
low genetic variation, increasing the risk of disease from a [ _____ ].farmers replacing rubber trees with oil palms.severe [ _____ ] events.
Synthetic rubber
can be used in engine components and kitchen products.is not as [ _____ ] as the natural material.cannot be used for several applications, including aircraft tyres.
Another possible source of natural rubber

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about current and possible future sources of rubber. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. A large proportion of the world's population now depends on industrial society and that society could not function without certain natural materials.

[00:58] AUDIO: Three resources are fundamental. The first is metal. Without it, we couldn't build machinery or modern transport. The second is fossil fuel, which supplies the energy those machines need.

[01:10] AUDIO: The third is rubber. It joins and protects mechanical components and items such as belts, tubing, and shock absorbers. Today, more than 40,000 different goods contain rubber, ranging from waterproof shoes to medical gloves. Two main forms of rubber are widely used.

[01:30] AUDIO: Almost all natural rubber is obtained from the para rubber tree. Although the species originated in Brazil, it is now grown commercially on plantations across Southeast Asia. There is increasing concern, however, that future production may not be enough to meet worldwide needs. So why is the quantity available so restricted?

[01:51] AUDIO: To begin with, rubber trees take a long time to mature. A newly planted tree may need eight to ten years before it yields any latex, which makes the whole cultivation process slow. This creates a second difficulty. Growers of many other crops can respond fairly quickly when demand rises or falls by changing what they plant or how much they produce.

[02:17] AUDIO: Rubber farmers must make those decisions many years in advance, so output cannot easily be adjusted to changes in demand. The tree is also extremely particular about its surroundings. It requires a suitable combination of heat, rainfall, and altitude. Because those conditions are not found in the far north or south, commercial cultivation is restricted to the region around the equator.

[02:44] AUDIO: Harvesting has changed very little over centuries. Workers cut shallow channels into each trunk and place a small container beneath them to collect the liquid latex. Every tree has to be treated by hand, so obtaining the raw material requires a great deal of labor. Limitations continue after the rubber has been used.

[03:06] AUDIO: Materials such as glass and water can often be recovered and reused. Rubber can technically be processed in this way too, but it is extremely difficult to recycle. As a result, relatively little returns to the available supply. More recently, additional dangers have emerged.

[03:30] AUDIO: Nearly all the trees cultivated in Southeast Asia descend from a very small collection of seeds originally brought from Brazil. Their genetic variation is therefore limited, leaving plantations highly exposed to disease. The greatest biological risk is a fungus. It previously destroyed enormous numbers of trees in Brazil and could severely damage plantations in every producing region.

[03:58] AUDIO: Economic change is another concern. More farmers in Southeast Asia are replacing rubber trees with oil palms, because palm oil is simpler to produce and brings them greater profit. In addition, the region has repeatedly experienced extreme weather events, a pattern that is expected to continue. Natural rubber is not the only option, since rubber can also be manufactured synthetically.

[04:25] AUDIO: The artificial product performs well in some applications, including components for engines and silicone kitchenware. Its weakness is that it is nowhere near as strong as natural rubber, so it cannot be substituted in every product. Car tires can use a blend of the two materials. Aircraft tires are different.

[04:46] AUDIO: During takeoff and landing, they experience exceptional speeds and forces, and only natural rubber can tolerate those conditions reliably. This is why researchers have spent years searching for other plants that could supply natural rubber. One candidate may appear surprising. It is a yellow-flowered wild plant commonly treated as a garden weed, a type of dandelion.

[05:12] AUDIO: When the plant is pulled from the ground and its roots are cut, rubber can be found inside them. Individual dandelions yield much less rubber than a tree, but they have an important advantage. They are highly adaptable. They can be cultivated in a wide range of places and do not require fertile soil.

[05:34] AUDIO: Several research programs are therefore examining whether dandelions could become a practical rubber crop. A further possibility is a desert shrub found in Mexico and Texas. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

content:
CourseDateCostNotesVietnamese food[ _____ ]£59Explains different ways of cooking with herbs. 

No places are currently available.Bread making20 March£[ _____ ]Ingredients cost extra. 

Students prepare white bread, sourdough and [ _____ ].Face massage23 February£35The instructor completed her training in [ _____ ]. 

Students must bring a [ _____ ].Candle making[ _____ ]£52The candles are made entirely from [ _____ ] materials and are suitable as gifts.Silk painting18 May£[ _____ ]Wear an apron or bring an old [ _____ ] to protect your clothes.DIY for beginners24 February£125Learn to use a drill, a saw and a [ _____ ], then attach a shelf to a wall.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking a college administrator about several one-day courses. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:46] MAN: Good morning, Steinford College external course registration. How may I help?

[00:52] WOMAN: Hi. I'm calling about the one-day classes being offered next year. A leaflet arrived in the post, but I can't find it now. I've heard that several courses are almost full, so I thought I should make a decision soon.
[01:06] MAN: Of course. Do you recall which course first caught your attention?

[01:12] WOMAN: There were several. One was about preparing Vietnamese food, which sounded appealing. If I remember correctly, it takes place on the 13th of January, and the price was roughly 60 pounds.

[01:25] MAN: The date is correct, but the exact fee is 59 pounds. The class is extremely popular. Among other topics, the tutor demonstrates the different ways herbs are used in Vietnamese cooking. Unfortunately, every place has currently been booked, although I could add your name to the waiting list.
[01:46] WOMAN: No, that's all right. I was also considering the bread-making course. Is that held sometime in March?
[01:53] MAN: Yes, on the 20th of March. Would you like me to reserve a place?
[01:58] WOMAN: I haven't decided yet. What's the fee?
[02:01] MAN: The course itself costs 48 pounds. You also pay separately for the ingredients. I don't know the precise amount for those, but I believe it's no more than 20 pounds.
[02:14] WOMAN: What do participants actually prepare?
[02:16] MAN: Several things. They bake white bread and sourdough, which has become very fashionable. And they also learn to make pizza. I'm told the result is excellent.
[02:27] WOMAN: I'd certainly enjoy that. There were a few other options in the leaflet too. Wasn't there a class in facial massage? I'd really like to learn the technique.
[02:37] MAN: There is. It's on the 23rd of February and costs 35 pounds for the day. The tutor is very good. She teaches a traditional method used in India and completed her own training there.
[02:52] MAN: It's intended to relax the face and reduce lines and wrinkles. Since you practice on yourself, you need to bring a mirror so you can watch what you're doing.
[03:04] WOMAN: Fine.
[03:08] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:50] WOMAN: I also seem to remember a candle making course.
[03:53] MAN: Yes, that one is in April. Let me confirm the day. It's the 6th. It was originally arranged for the 23rd of January, but the college had to move it.

[04:04] MAN: The charge is 52 pounds. It's another course that fills quickly, although a small number of places remain. One reason for its popularity is that the candles are produced entirely from natural materials.
[04:19] WOMAN: A friend of mine took it and said the finished candles were ideal as gifts. She actually gave one to me.

[04:27] MAN: Have you considered silk painting as well? That class is scheduled for the 18th of May. Students create patterns on silk and add color with special dyes. The finished work can be framed as a picture or turned into something practical, such as a scarf.
[04:46] MAN: It costs 67 pounds 50, which seems good value. I've seen a comparable course advertised for 110 pounds.
[04:56] WOMAN: That sounds interesting. Would I have to supply the silk myself?
[05:01] MAN: No. You only need something that will keep the dye off your clothes. You can bring an apron, if you own one, or an old shirt, because the colors can leave permanent stains.
[05:14] WOMAN: Right. The final course I was thinking about was rather different. DIY for beginners. I'd like to become capable of doing simple repairs around the house.
[05:26] WOMAN: Does that still have spaces?
[05:28] MAN: Yes, a few. It runs on the 24th of February. The fee is higher, at 125 pounds, but it remains very popular. You'll be shown how to operate an electric drill and a saw.
[05:43] WOMAN: That would be useful. I even need someone to teach me how to handle a hammer, because I usually hit my fingers.
[05:49] MAN: The class covers that, too. After learning to use the essential tools safely, everyone completes a practical task, attaching a shelf to a wall.
[06:02] WOMAN: Perfect. That's exactly what I need. I'd like to enrol for that course, and also for…
[06:09] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Melby Coal Mine
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Melby Coal Mine"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide giving visitors information about two local walks and the Melby coal mine site. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. I'm going to tell you about two history and nature walks in this area.

[00:55] AUDIO: Each can be finished in under a day, and either one can be combined with a visit to Melby, a former coal mine which now welcomes visitors. The Marsden Coastal Walk is manageable for families because it involves no demanding climbs. It begins at Marsden Harbour. Ferries leave there every hour for Hooker Island, which is popular with anglers, but the walk itself follows part of the coastal trail.

[01:24] AUDIO: Direction signs are positioned all along the route, so there's really no need to carry a map. The path briefly turns inland and passes the remains of a 15th century castle. The market town that once stood nearby has completely disappeared, but the castle ruins are well worth seeing, and information panels show how the building used to look. Anyone who starts early should be back by lunchtime.

[01:53] AUDIO: The Melby Heritage Walk is particularly popular with photographers after dark. At certain times of year, visitors travel considerable distances to climb above the valley and photograph the stars. During the day, however, the woodland at the bottom of the valley is so peaceful that you may hear nothing except your own footsteps. After the climb, the highest point offers a broad view.

[02:21] AUDIO: Energetic walkers can also go up the tower built on the site of a 17th-century hunting lodge. From there, the path follows the hilltops before descending to the same car park at Melby Coal Mine, where the walk began. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[03:25] AUDIO: Melby Coal Mine has been open to the public for 20 years and has received awards for the quality of the visit. Several original mine buildings survive and most now contain displays. I'll describe the plan starting from the car park. Follow the covered walkway into the main visitor centre and pass through the ticket office.

[03:49] AUDIO: The next small area has lockers for heavy bags and raincoats visitors can borrow. Continue beyond that room into the larger space. That is where you'll find the historical exhibition, including many original black and white photographs. The miner's bathhouse is the small building immediately north of the engine house.

[04:13] AUDIO: Its boiler has been removed, but rows of tin baths remain on the stone floor. The collection of early hand tools is in the L-shaped building, halfway along the northern edge of the site. The display shows how miners cut through rock before mechanised equipment was introduced. Mining vehicles are displayed in the long building in the southwest corner.

[04:40] AUDIO: It contains wagons of several sizes, as well as advanced cutting machines used shortly before the mine closed. And you reach it by a covered walkway. Children usually enjoy the pony field. It occupies the northeastern boundary, and unlike the vehicle display, it is not reached by a covered walkway.

[05:05] AUDIO: Finally, the education centre is the L-shaped building near the centre. School groups use it, but other visitors can enter because it also contains a library and a small gift shop. A short covered section connects it directly with the ticket office. That is the end of part two.
[05:27] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Sessions on food safety
content: 📌 Student project: developing a new food product
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two food science students discussing their course and a recent project with their tutor. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:48] TUTOR: Thanks for meeting me, Nadia and Fergus. I'd like to hear what you thought about different parts of the course. Where shall we start?
[00:57] NADIA: I really liked the food safety sessions. Some of the figures were unexpected, although other points were familiar. For instance, I already knew obesity was becoming more common.
[01:08] FERGUS: So did I. It's reported quite often. What surprised me was learning that contaminated food can cause more than 200 separate illnesses.
[01:16] NADIA: Yes. I had no idea the figure was anywhere near that high. I knew that resistance to antibiotics was increasing, but I hadn't understood what was contributing to it.
[01:27] FERGUS: One cause is the use of antibiotics in livestock. When those animals later enter the human food chain, the drugs can do so as well. That connection was completely new to me.
[01:39] NADIA: Me too. We also heard a lot about plastic from food packaging reaching the sea, but I think everyone in the class had encountered that issue before.
[01:47] FERGUS: And food waste deserved more attention. We already hear plenty about edible food being thrown away because people mistrust date labels, but the lecturer only referred to it briefly.
[01:57] TUTOR: I'll note that. Fergus, how useful were the sessions led by visiting speakers?
[02:04] FERGUS: The best one for me described a project designed to stop food producers giving customers false information.
[02:10] TUTOR: The food fraud project?
[02:11] FERGUS: That's right. I was impressed that it considered so many kinds of consumer. It covered people following religious food rules, vegetarians and vegans, and those who have allergies.
[02:24] NADIA: The scientific side was interesting too.

[02:26] FERGUS: Yes, though DNA analysis itself isn't recent, reliable techniques have existed for some time. The clever part was arranging for food to be tested repeatedly at different points between the producer and the customer.
[02:40] NADIA: That meant they could check both where a product came from and whether it contained the ingredients shown on the label.
[02:46] FERGUS: Exactly. So buyers had stronger evidence about what they were purchasing.
[02:51] NADIA: The research team also tried to make its findings public.
[02:54] FERGUS: They did, but that part wasn't handled particularly well. The information didn't reach as many people as it should have.
[03:01] TUTOR: Alright. Are there any subjects you both think we should add to the course?
[03:06] NADIA: I'd like to examine ways of raising crop yields without harming the natural environment.
[03:11] FERGUS: We've already spent quite a lot of time on sustainable farming. We've done far less on the fishing industry, and the risk of taking fish faster than stocks can recover.

[03:20] NADIA: I agree. Protecting those stocks would make an excellent topic. Another possibility is nutrition designed around the needs of each person, now that technology can analyze those needs accurately.
[03:32] FERGUS: I'm not convinced. That seems closer to medicine than to food science.
[03:37] NADIA: Fair enough. We could compare what people eat in different parts of the world and how consumption patterns vary.
[03:44] FERGUS: Yes, that would be relevant. And I'm sure the rest of the class would be interested as well.
[03:49] NADIA: What about digital development, such as food produced by 3D printers or intelligent packaging?
[03:55] FERGUS: Perhaps, though I think that may be too specialized for this course.
[04:02] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:45] TUTOR: I'd also like to discuss your project in which you developed a new food product. Tell me how you approached each stage. First, you had to agree on the overall aim.
[04:56] FERGUS: We wanted to make something people could eat while traveling rather than only at a table in a restaurant.
[05:01] NADIA: So we chose falafel, the snack that originally came from the Middle East.
[05:07] FERGUS: We settled on both the aim and the product very quickly. Other groups apparently struggled with that decision and lost quite a lot of time, but we didn't.
[05:16] NADIA: The next stage was the literature review. Neither of us had written one before, so the project handbook was extremely helpful.
[05:24] FERGUS: Especially the section explaining how the material should be organized and presented.
[05:28] TUTOR: Then you moved on to developing the product itself.
[05:32] FERGUS: Yes, we had to choose the ingredients, and we wanted our version to be noticeably different from standard falafel.
[05:39] NADIA: Eventually, we selected jackfruit. It was completely unfamiliar to us because neither of us had ever tasted it.
[05:46] FERGUS: Although it's a fruit, it works surprisingly well in savory food.
[05:50] TUTOR: And what happened when you began producing the falafel?
[05:52] FERGUS: Finding a reliable method was more demanding than I'd expected, since I'd never made it before.
[05:59] NADIA: We used a basic recipe first and then changed it through trial and error. Several attempts failed, so we kept adjusting the mixture.
[06:07] FERGUS: It was certainly challenging, but we enjoyed experimenting and the final version worked well. Yes, the whole process was great fun.
[06:15] TUTOR: Thank you. That gives me a very clear picture of your project.
[06:22] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.
