passages.title: Challenges facing the cruise ship industry
content: 📌 Challenges facing the cruise ship industry
Problems caused by overtourism

[ _____ ] is described as one of the most serious issues.Some cities, including Barcelona, have introduced a visitor [ _____ ] in an attempt to lower tourist numbers.Bruges restricted day trips from the nearby port because the city was beginning to resemble a theme park; many shops mainly sold [ _____ ] and souvenirs.Dubrovnik controls tourist numbers by managing the [ _____ ] of cruise ships entering its port.
Problems with the industry’s image
Cruise holidays are commonly linked with older people.Many younger travellers have an incorrect impression of their [ _____ ].Potential passengers believe they will have to follow too many [ _____ ].

How cruise companies are responding
Cruise lines are trying to attract younger customers by:

improving sustainability, for example through hybrid enginesproviding varied activities such as boxing, [ _____ ] and well+being sessionsupdating menus to include [ _____ ] choicesguaranteeing dependable [ _____ ]using professionally produced [ _____ ] on social media
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a presentation about difficulties affecting the cruise industry and how cruise companies are responding. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today, I'm going to examine several challenges facing the cruise ship industry, followed by some possible responses.

[00:54] AUDIO: In recent decades, cruise travel has contributed to overtourism, which occurs when visitor numbers become so high that they damage a destination. Pollution is among the most serious problems created in many popular locations. The situation is complicated because cities and islands want the income and publicity that tourism brings, yet many cannot manage thousands of cruise passengers arriving every day. Heavy visitor numbers can gradually spoil the scenery and attractions that drew people there.

[01:26] AUDIO: Barcelona and several other cities have reacted by introducing a tax for passengers who come ashore from cruise ships. The charge is only a few euros, however, so environmental groups doubt that it will reduce numbers significantly. Bruges faced a similar issue. At busy times, day visitors traveling from the Port of Zebrugge made it extremely difficult to move through the city.

[01:47] AUDIO: Some residents felt that the historic center was turning into a theme park because shops were serving tourists almost exclusively, offering chocolate, for which Belgium is famous, together with souvenirs. The council therefore took steps to restrict cruise day trips to a more manageable level. Dubrovnik also became an exceptionally popular cruise destination after appearing in a successful television series. Rather than allowing several ships to arrive together, the authorities now control the timing of entries into the port.

[02:19] AUDIO: Even so, some local people believe stronger limits are still required. Cruise ships are not only criticized by destinations, they also suffer from a problem of perception. They have traditionally been regarded as safe holidays for elderly people, with relatively little to interest younger couples or families. A recent survey found that cost is another major reason younger adults avoid cruises.

[02:46] AUDIO: Many assume they are expensive, although a cruise may offer good value compared with other packaged holidays because drinks and activities are often included. There is also a widespread belief that passengers must follow numerous rules about dress and behavior. In reality, most modern cruises are far less formal than they once were. So how can cruise companies change these attitudes and appeal to younger travelers?

[03:11] AUDIO: One advantage they now promote is greater sustainability. Some newly built ships use hybrid engines and large batteries, which allow the main engines to be switched off while the vessel is in port. Companies are also creating ships specifically for passengers aged between 21 and 45. The interiors are contemporary and the activities are unlike those on a traditional cruise.

[03:32] AUDIO: One vessel even has a boxing ring while many organize diving trips. At the same time, extensive well-being programs offer several kinds of session. Food remains central to the cruise experience, so menus have been modernized to reflect younger customers' preferences. Vegan choices, for example, are now standard.

[03:53] AUDIO: Many onboard restaurants have also removed printed menus and display them on screens instead. Older passengers sometimes chose a cruise in order to disconnect from everyday life. Younger travelers, by contrast, expect constant contact with friends and relatives. On longer voyages, some passengers also continue working, which means companies must provide Wi-Fi that remains reliable throughout the trip.

[04:17] AUDIO: Marketing has changed as well. My grandparents enjoyed browsing cruise brochures even when they had no plans to travel, while television advertising until recently looked old-fashioned and seemed directed at retired people. Cruise operators were slow to recognize the influence of social media, but leading companies now hire specialist agencies to create professional videos for their online channels. Whether these environmental, onboard, and marketing changes are enough to reshape the industry's future remains to be seen.
[04:50] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear Tammy asking Paul for advice about travelling by ferry to the Shetland Islands. First, you have some time to look at questions one to four. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to four.
[00:44] TAMMY: Paul, when you visited the Shetland Islands last year, did your family fly there or take the ferry?
[00:50] PAUL: We travelled by ferry, Tammy. I'd much rather drive than fly, and the crossing made the journey feel like part of the holiday.
[00:58] TAMMY: Which company did you book with?
[01:00] PAUL: There's just one operator on that route, Northern Ferries. All their services depart from Aberdeen.
[01:06] TAMMY: Do they run very often?

[01:08] PAUL: The timetable is fairly limited. During the summer, a boat leaves each evening, so that means seven sailings a week. I don't know the exact winter schedule, but it may drop to only four or five days.
[01:23] TAMMY: So you travel overnight? I like the thought of setting off in the evening and reaching the islands the next morning. What did the tickets cost?
[01:32] PAUL: Much less than I expected. The total for four passengers in our car came to just under £250.
[01:39] TAMMY: That's good. I'd imagined it would be closer to £400 in the busier season.
[01:46] PAUL: I thought the same, but it was excellent value. You should still reserve early because places fill quickly, particularly in the school holidays.
[01:56] TAMMY: The trouble is that our plans aren't completely certain. What happens if we cancel?
[02:01] PAUL: They don't normally return your money. Instead, you receive a voucher to use for a later journey, and you only qualify for that if you cancel at least one month beforehand.
[02:13] TAMMY: Then we'll have to decide soon.
[02:18] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions five to ten. Now listen and answer questions five to ten.
[03:01] TAMMY: Would you recommend reserving a cabin?

[03:03] PAUL: Definitely. We left it too late and couldn't get one with a window. Those cabins cost more, but they're much more pleasant than the ones inside the ship. A cabin isn't compulsory, though.
[03:14] PAUL: I think it's worth the extra money. There are also luxury cabins for two people with a television, but I wouldn't pay for one of those.
[03:22] TAMMY: Neither would I.
[03:23] PAUL: Make sure you pack snacks for the children as well. There isn't much choice on board, and most of the food isn't particularly healthy.
[03:30] TAMMY: Could they use the Wi-Fi to keep themselves occupied?
[03:34] PAUL: The connection was poor, so take some books for them instead.
[03:38] TAMMY: We might also have to bring our dog if nobody can care for him.
[03:41] PAUL: We took ours. The kennels are reasonably spacious and perfectly adequate, but owners have to supply a blanket.
[03:50] TAMMY: That sounds straightforward.
[03:51] PAUL: It was. The children thought the overnight crossing was a real adventure. Once morning came, they stood outside watching for dolphins, and we saw a large number of them.
[04:03] TAMMY: Mine would really enjoy that.
[04:05] PAUL: Here's another suggestion. We reached Aberdeen several hours before departure. So rather than waiting at the terminal, we went somewhere nearby.
[04:14] TAMMY: Where did you choose?
[04:15] PAUL: Drum Castle.
[04:17] TAMMY: Drum, as in the musical instrument?
[04:19] PAUL: Exactly. It's worth seeing if you have enough time. There's an impressive tower, attractive gardens, and some very old woodland.
[04:28] TAMMY: Is there somewhere to have a proper meal?
[04:30] PAUL: The castle only has a coffee shop, not a restaurant. We searched the surrounding area and found a very good Italian restaurant in a nearby village. I can look up its name for you.
[04:42] TAMMY: Thanks, Paul. That would be really helpful.
[04:48] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Popularity of street food
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Popularity of street food"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a street food business owner giving advice to people who are considering starting a similar business. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good evening.

[00:49] AUDIO: I'm John and I own VEGOUT, a mobile business specializing in vegan food. Since 2012 I've traveled around the country in a converted van cooking at outdoor events of many kinds. This evening, I'd like to pass on some lessons from that experience. This is an excellent time to enter the industry because public interest in street food is still increasing.

[01:15] AUDIO: In my view, there are two main reasons. Street food offers an alternative to conventional fast food. Fast food may be inexpensive and widely available, but it tends to be unhealthy and almost identical wherever you buy it. Street food stalls by contrast can offer everything from premium burgers to vegan curries.

[01:42] AUDIO: Customers enjoy discovering something unusual that isn't available everywhere else. They also value freshness. They can watch their meal being made in front of them rather than receiving food taken directly from a freezer. Choosing the right selling location is essential.

[02:01] AUDIO: Beginners often assume a music festival is the natural choice, yet pitches there can be extremely expensive and competition is intense. A food market is much more suitable. The visitors are already interested in what they eat and they often give useful comments about new dishes. A space in a local park is another very good option.

[02:25] AUDIO: The atmosphere is relaxed, while the number of people walking past can provide a steady flow of customers. After your business develops a reputation, you may be invited to cater for parties. These are enjoyable, but demanding. Street food is fashionable at weddings as well, though I wouldn't suggest starting there because every detail has to be right.

[02:55] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Opening a mobile food business is cheaper than launching a restaurant or cafe, but you still need basic appliances. My advice is to buy used hobs and fridges at first.

[03:49] AUDIO: If the business succeeds, you can replace them later with higher-quality models. Hiring equipment may appear economical, but over time it usually costs more. You probably already know what kind of food you want to sell. You may have checked whether a similar product is available nearby and considered allergies to ingredients such as eggs or nuts.
[04:13] AUDIO: One detail that beginners sometimes overlook is presentation. Will customers receive the food on a plate or in a bag? Will they need a fork? Can the packaging be recycled or reused?

[04:27] AUDIO: The product must be simple to eat and visually attractive if you want people to return. Even with careful planning, every new operation encounters difficulties. I'll describe four examples from businesses I know. The friends who established High Basil continued working in a restaurant while launching their food truck.

[04:50] AUDIO: They finished at the restaurant around midnight throughout the week, then spent their days off selling at markets. As a result, the hours they worked were enormous and they had almost no personal time. Basque depended on fish for several dishes, but the ingredient became so expensive that the owners struggled to make a profit. Customers would not accept a large price increase, so the menu had to shift away from fish and include more vegetarian choices.

[05:24] AUDIO: Lou's kitchen prepared salads individually inside its van, and some recipes involved several stages. At one early event, orders took so long that the queue lasted more than 15 minutes. Many customers became impatient and left. Whatever you sell must therefore be assembled and served efficiently.

[05:48] AUDIO: Chip Chop identified an ideal position close to a beach with no other food vans nearby. Unfortunately, the owners discovered that selling there required a special permit, unlike operating at a market or festival. Securing it involved such a complicated procedure that they eventually abandoned the location. I hope those examples have given you a realistic sense of both the opportunities and the practical challenges involved in running a street food business.
[06:25] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Ethical and sustainable fashion
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Ethical and sustainable fashion"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two textile students discussing research for a project on ethical and sustainable fashion. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:48] STUDENT 1: Shall we review the research for our sustainable fashion project?
[00:52] STUDENT 2: Yes. I think I've read enough material now.
[00:55] STUDENT 1: So, have I? And I understand the idea of sustainability much better than I did before.
[01:00] STUDENT 2: My reading focused more on ethical fashion. Before this project, I hadn't clearly recognized how that differed from sustainable fashion.

[01:11] STUDENT 1: That confusion is very common. People regularly treat the two expressions as if they mean the same thing, although their main concerns are different. Sustainable fashion mainly deals with environmental effects, whereas ethical fashion focuses more on how workers and animals are treated.

[01:29] STUDENT 2: It's understandable that people mix them up because the industry uses so many related expressions. Eco-friendly. For example, sounds positive but tells consumers almost nothing specific.

[01:44] STUDENT 1: Companies make the problem worse when they describe products with broad claims but give very little detail about the production process. The language is often vague enough to create a misleading impression.
[01:56] STUDENT 2: I agree.
[01:58] STUDENT 1: The debate over wool was especially interesting. Wool is widely presented as sustainable because it is a natural material.

[02:06] STUDENT 2: It is certainly durable, and the fiber can be recycled which are genuine advantages. But I don't accept the claim that producing wool requires hardly any chemicals. Sheep farming uses fungicides and insecticides, among other treatments.
[02:22] STUDENT 1: Exactly. I also search for evidence that sheep cause less environmental harm than cattle, but I couldn't find anything convincing.

[02:32] STUDENT 2: Neither species has a good environmental record. I found conflicting views about shearing, too. Some reports call it cruel, but provided sheep are healthy and properly cared for, I don't see shearing itself as unethical.
[02:48] STUDENT 1: Nor do I.
[02:51] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:34] STUDENT 2: Let's move on to the newer semi-synthetic materials.
[03:39] STUDENT 1: Alright.

[03:39] STUDENT 2: First, lyocell, which is made from eucalyptus pulp. Its manufacturing system is impressive because more than 99% of the dissolving chemicals are recovered and reused rather than discarded.
[03:53] STUDENT 1: Kupro was new to me. It uses waste from cotton production to create a material similar to silk but suitable for vegans.
[04:03] STUDENT 2: Unfortunately, its environmental performance is poor. Reports repeatedly link the manufacturing process with serious pollution.
[04:12] STUDENT 1: Compared with the other alternative fabrics we studied, Kupro appears to be the least sustainable.
[04:18] STUDENT 2: Bamboo is much more familiar, but the label alone can be misleading. Only bamboo processed organically can genuinely be regarded as sustainable.
[04:29] STUDENT 1: Yes. A large proportion is manufactured through chemical-intensive methods that can cause considerable environmental damage.
[04:38] STUDENT 2: Ecoverro is another semi-synthetic fabric, and demand for it is rising quickly.

[04:44] STUDENT 1: That may be because producing it creates about 50% fewer emissions and consumes only half the energy required for conventional material. Lower energy use also reduces manufacturing costs.
[04:59] STUDENT 2: Cork should become more popular, too. It works particularly well for vegan footwear and bags.
[05:05] STUDENT 1: Cork is unusual because the source is completely sustainable. Cork trees are renewable while the finished material is both recyclable and biodegradable.
[05:16] STUDENT 2: Harvesting the bark can even benefit the trees, so the source has no significant environmental disadvantage.
[05:24] STUDENT 1: Hemp is another promising fabric derived from a natural plant.
[05:28] STUDENT 2: It also offers benefits to the person wearing it. Hemp clothing provides some protection from sunlight and has antibacterial properties.
[05:38] STUDENT 1: I hadn't known that. I did learn that the plant can be difficult to cultivate, which may explain why the fabric is not yet more widespread.
[05:47] STUDENT 2: That could change as interest in these alternative materials continues to grow.

passages.title: Invasive species.
content: 📌 Invasive species
Definition: a plant or animal introduced by people which then damages its new environment
Ways an invasive species may cause harm
It may eat native organisms.It can bring an unfamiliar [ _____ ].It may compete with native species for food.It can put the survival of an entire [ _____ ] at risk.
How invasive species reach new areas
accidentally, for example on people returning from their [ _____ ] or in ship cargodeliberately, for pest control or to be kept as [ _____ ]

Examples
Rhinella marina toads

They were brought from Hawaii to Australia in 1935 to control beetles damaging [ _____ ] crops.They did not solve the original problem and spread throughout northern Australia.Their poison kills predators, while their numbers reduce food for native frogs.
Other examples in the UK

Japanese knotweed was once valued by nineteenth+century gardeners.Rhododendrons stop [ _____ ] from reaching plants beneath them.Grey squirrels compete with red squirrels for food and carry a deadly [ _____ ].
Controlling invasive species

Monitoring provides information about their [ _____ ] and environmental effects.A nationwide [ _____ ] allows organisations to share records and track them.The public can help by being asked to [ _____ ] suspected invasive species and report sightings.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of an ecology lecture about invasive plants and animals. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today's topic is invasive species.

[00:49] AUDIO: I'll begin by clarifying the definition. An invasive species is a plant or animal introduced into an environment through human activity which then causes harm there. Not every non-native species is invasive. Many survive in a new region without creating serious problems.

[01:10] AUDIO: In the most severe cases, an invasive organism can transform an environment almost completely. It may prey on native wildlife or bring a disease that local species have never encountered and cannot resist. It may also reproduce rapidly and consume resources that native species depend on. Biological invasions are among the major causes of damage to an ecosystem and can even threaten its continued survival.

[01:43] AUDIO: How do these organisms reach new places? Human activity is by far the main cause, either accidentally or deliberately. Someone returning from a holiday abroad may unknowingly carry plant seeds, on clothing or footwear. Insects and other organisms can also travel within cargo or on the outside of ships, then escape after arrival.

[02:10] AUDIO: People sometimes transport a species intentionally. It might be released to control agricultural pests or imported to keep as pets. Difficulties arise if these organisms enter the wild and reproduce or spread in ways nobody anticipated. A well-known Australian example is the toad Rhinella marina.

[02:33] AUDIO: It was brought from Hawaii in 1935 as a biological control. The plan was for the toads to eat grey-backed beetles that were destroying sugar crops on plantations. Scientists initially released only a small number in Queensland, but other states soon copied the program. Within two years, 62,000 young toads had entered the wild.

[02:59] AUDIO: The toads failed to protect the plantations, yet they multiplied quickly and spread across northern Australia. They are poisonous throughout their life cycle, so animals that eat them can die. Their large population also leaves less food available for native frogs. The United Kingdom provides several further examples and has more than 3,000 invasive species.

[03:29] AUDIO: Japanese knotweed was admired by 19th-century gardeners as an ornamental plant. Once it escaped into the countryside, however, it spread aggressively and proved extremely difficult to remove. Rhododendrons were introduced even earlier and now grow in many British parks and woods. Their dense growth blocks so much light that native wildflowers cannot survive underneath.

[04:00] AUDIO: Grey squirrels were brought from North America to private estates during the 19th century. They are now widespread in both woodland and towns. These squirrels compete with the smaller native red squirrel for the same food. More seriously, grey squirrels carry a virus which is fatal to red squirrels.

[04:22] AUDIO: As a result, red squirrel numbers have fallen dramatically, and only a few populations remain. So, what can ecologists do about invasive species? The first priority is to study the behaviour of a newly arrived organism. Continued monitoring reveals whether it is beginning to damage its new surroundings and how its population is changing.

[04:49] AUDIO: A national database is an effective way to record and track invasive species. Relevant agencies can add observations, share information and coordinate any action required. Members of the public are valuable in this work too. They can be encouraged to photograph a suspected harmful species to help identification, then report where and when it was seen.

[05:18] AUDIO: People should not touch or attempt to destroy the organism themselves. Together, careful monitoring, shared records and public reporting can support a faster response when a harmful new species appears.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear an interviewer who is carrying out a survey about shopping in Broad Beach. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:46] INTERVIEWER: Good afternoon. I'm asking people about their shopping habits in Broad Beach. Would you mind answering a few questions?
[00:54] RACHEL: That's fine as long as it doesn't take too long. I need to get back to work soon.
[01:00] INTERVIEWER: It should only take a few minutes. Could I begin with your name?
[01:04] RACHEL: Rachel Keating.
[01:05] INTERVIEWER: Thank you. Is your surname K-E-E-T-I-N-G?
[01:09] RACHEL: Not quite. It begins with K-E-A then T-I-N-G. Keating.
[01:16] INTERVIEWER: Right, I've got that. We use names only to keep the survey form separate. Now how did you travel into the town center today?
[01:25] RACHEL: I usually take the tram because parking is difficult. But the weather was so good this morning that I came on my bicycle.
[01:32] INTERVIEWER: So you didn't use public transport today?
[01:36] RACHEL: No. The bicycle was quicker actually because the tram was delayed.
[01:40] INTERVIEWER: And what brought you into Broad Beach today? Have you been shopping already?
[01:45] RACHEL: I've done one appointment. I've just come from the optician where I had my eyes tested. I thought I might need new glasses, but fortunately I don't.
[01:54] INTERVIEWER: That's good news. Is there anything you still need to buy?
[01:59] RACHEL: Yes. I'm going to a conference next month, and at first I thought I needed a whole suit. But my trousers are fine, so I'm really looking for a new jacket.
[02:09] INTERVIEWER: I see. Any other errands while you're here?
[02:13] RACHEL: I have to collect my camera from the repair shop. The screen stopped working last week. They said it might take 10 days, but they phoned yesterday to say the camera was ready.
[02:23] INTERVIEWER: At least it was repaired quickly.
[02:26] RACHEL: Yes. Although I've been using my phone for photographs in the meantime.
[02:31] INTERVIEWER: Today is Friday. Is Friday normally your favorite day to shop?

[02:35] RACHEL: No. Fridays get rather crowded after lunch. I sometimes come on Monday if I need groceries, but Wednesday is the day I prefer. I finish work early then, and most of the shops stay open until 6.
[02:49] INTERVIEWER: Thanks.
[02:52] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[03:34] INTERVIEWER: I'd also like your opinion of shopping in the town center. How do you find the staff in the shops?
[03:41] RACHEL: Very good. Even when a shop is busy, the assistants usually take time to help. I'd describe the service as excellent.
[03:50] INTERVIEWER: What about the range of shops? Some people say the center has changed a lot recently.
[03:56] RACHEL: It has. We've gained several cafes which are useful if you want a hot drink, and three new places selling sandwiches. That's excessive. One sandwich shop would have been enough.
[04:08] INTERVIEWER: So there are too many sandwich outlets. What kind of shop would you rather have?

[04:14] RACHEL: We already have plenty of clothes shops and a couple of good gift shops. What's missing is somewhere practical. There's only one small shop where you can buy stationary, and its range is poor. I'd like another place selling that.
[04:29] INTERVIEWER: Have you visited the new shopping center outside Broad Beach?
[04:33] RACHEL: Twice. It's easy to reach from my neighborhood, and I like the way the building has been designed.
[04:39] INTERVIEWER: The glass entrance has received a lot of attention.

[04:42] RACHEL: Yes, and the roof brings in plenty of light. But the fountains in the central courtyard are my favorite feature. Children can play beside them, and they make the whole place feel cooler.
[04:56] INTERVIEWER: The center also has several leisure facilities. What do you think of those?

[05:01] RACHEL: The cinema is useful because it shows films the one in town doesn't, but I don't understand why they built a gym there. Broad Beach already has a larger sports center nearby with lower membership fees, so the gym seems unnecessary.
[05:17] INTERVIEWER: That covers everything. Thank you for your help, Rachel.
[05:20] RACHEL: You're welcome.

passages.title: James Craig's business exhibition
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "James Craig's business exhibition"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a podcast about an annual business exhibition. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Welcome to the Enterprise Exchange podcast.

[00:50] AUDIO: Our exhibition returns to London next month, bringing together independent companies, advisors, and experienced business leaders. Today, I'll explain what exhibitors can expect and introduce this year's guest speakers. I'll begin with some comments from James Craig, the founder of ClearCall, a company that provides communication systems for small offices. James has exhibited with us for two years.

[01:17] AUDIO: James says that during his first visit, ClearCall had a stand in the Enterprise Hall. It was a good place to meet potential customers, although there wasn't enough room to demonstrate the equipment properly. Last year, the company moved its demonstrations to the Product Trial Lounge. Visitors could sit down, use the equipment, and compare different systems, so James intends to book that area again.

[01:45] AUDIO: ClearCall also paid to support the partnership hub last year. Companies posted details of the services they needed there, and James says this brought him several valuable contracts. Sponsoring the hub also made the ClearCall name much more visible. James considered the Innovation Lab last year, but decided it was aimed mainly at manufacturers.

[02:09] AUDIO: At the next exhibition, he hopes to give a short presentation on the startup stage, although that has not yet been confirmed. Exhibiting companies also receive access to our funds, and every employee of a company that books an exhibition space may use it. The scheme is not limited to the staff who actually attend the event. Savings are available on train and hotel bookings, as well as computers, printers, and other technology products.

[02:46] AUDIO: Food shops used to be included, but they left the scheme in January. The discounts vary from 4 to 18 percent, depending on the supplier. There is no minimum purchase. Last year, the average cardholder saved just over 300 pounds, but that figure is a result, not a spending requirement.

[03:08] AUDIO: Cards are issued to employees by name, so they cannot be passed to relatives. Full instructions will be sent to exhibitors after registration. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[04:03] AUDIO: Now, I'd like to introduce six of the speakers appearing at this year's event. First is Lena Brooks. She began with a single mobile bakery, expecting to add a second van after two or three years. Instead, demand rose so quickly that she was running 20 outlets within 18 months.

[04:24] AUDIO: Her session examines the strain this sudden growth placed on recruitment, training, and quality control, and what she would do differently now. Marcus Vale founded a successful software company while he was still at university. As profits increased, he created a program that gives a fixed share of annual earnings to local charities. His employees also receive paid time to volunteer.

[04:53] AUDIO: Marcus will explain how commercial targets and community support can strengthen one another. Priya Nair has managed businesses in a remarkable range of locations. She opened a catering service in Singapore, worked with a furniture producer in Sweden, and later advised a delivery company in Brazil. Her talk compares what she learned about customers, negotiations, and workplace expectations in these different countries.

[05:22] AUDIO: Daniel Moss is known for building online retail businesses, but his session will concentrate on a separate project. Four years ago, he established a center where unemployed adults can receive interview practice, digital skills training, and introductions to local employers. He'll discuss how companies can help people return to work. Emily Zhao is the chief executive of Northline Media.

[05:50] AUDIO: The company originally printed catalogs for retailers, but demand fell as its clients moved online. Emily gradually retrained her staff and changed Northline into a provider of digital product displays and customer data services. She'll focus on recognizing shifts in the market and reshaping a company before its old services become irrelevant. Our final speaker is Tom Reyes, a consultant who works with business owners.

[06:22] AUDIO: His workshop is not about accounting problems or recovering lost investment. Instead, it explores difficulties in people's private lives, such as family pressure, lack of confidence, and poor work life boundaries. Tom will demonstrate practical ways to deal with these issues without allowing them to damage a business. Details of times and rooms are available on the exhibition website.
[06:51] AUDIO: We hope to see you there.

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: In part 3, you will hear two students discussing a presentation about housing in the future. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
[00:49] MIA: Leo, you remember the presentation we're doing together this term?
[00:53] LEO: The one about homes in the future?
[00:55] MIA: Yes. I'm slightly worried about it. Do they expect us to invent completely new ideas for what those homes might be like?

[01:04] LEO: I don't think that's the aim. We're supposed to describe possible developments and assess them. The problem is, we can't just make broad claims. We'll need suitable real-life cases to back up every point, and finding enough of those could take quite a while.
[01:22] MIA: Yes, that's what concerns me too. When do we have to submit it?
[01:26] LEO: Not for another six weeks, so the deadline shouldn't be a problem.
[01:30] MIA: That's a relief. We should probably choose the kind of housing we're going to examine now.
[01:35] LEO: What about homes designed for several generations of the same family?
[01:40] MIA: Possibly. Or we could look at housing for people who live alone.
[01:45] LEO: I heard another pair have chosen that. I was thinking of accommodations specifically for older people, since demand for that is likely to rise.
[01:54] MIA: True, but your first idea about relatives of different ages sharing a home gives us more to discuss. Let's choose that.
[02:04] LEO: Fine. Most of the extra housing will probably be needed in cities. One possible response would be to turn existing office or industrial buildings into flats.

[02:14] MIA: Or designers could arrange the available space more imaginatively, allowing people to manage in smaller homes. Even so, I think the main answer is to build apartment blocks with many floors.
[02:27] LEO: So cities grow upwards rather than spreading out.
[02:31] MIA: I agree.
[02:34] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 24 to 30.
[03:18] MIA: Right. Let's move on to some particular features that future housing might include.
[03:23] LEO: We could start with gardens on the roofs of buildings, especially tower blocks.

[03:29] MIA: They wouldn't only work on tall buildings. A single-story suburban property could have one as well. But I think the people who'd gain most are those living high up in a city, because greenery nearby could make such a difference to their well-being.
[03:46] LEO: Particularly when their flat has no balcony.

[03:49] MIA: Exactly. Another feature could be a communal work area within the building or shared by a small group of houses. Residents working from home would have somewhere better to go than their kitchen table.
[04:04] LEO: They'd avoid the journey to an office, but still meet other people. Conversations with someone in a completely different line of work can produce ideas you wouldn't have had by yourself.
[04:16] MIA: I've also read about apartments with internal partitions that can be moved. The layout could then be altered as the household changes over the years.

[04:26] LEO: That could be useful when adult children remain at home after starting work, or if an older relative later comes to live with the family. Both the people already there and anyone joining them could have a space arranged for their own needs.
[04:41] MIA: What do you think of bathroom mirrors that can check a person's health? They're meant to identify possible symptoms and contact a doctor automatically.
[04:51] LEO: I'm not convinced that's sensible.
[04:54] MIA: Neither am I. They might make people anxious about something that turns out to be harmless.
[05:00] LEO: We should mention transport, too. Housing developments could provide secure bike stores with charging sockets, so residents could leave electric bicycles there and recharge them.
[05:12] MIA: Yes, that might persuade more people to cycle instead of driving, which would reduce the environmental impact.
[05:19] LEO: I came across a development where residents had to leave their cars at the edge, making the whole central area pedestrian only. It sounded ideal for families with young children.
[05:32] MIA: For them, perhaps. But it could be a real disadvantage for an older or disabled resident who couldn't walk very far.
[05:41] LEO: That's true.

[05:43] MIA: There was another scheme with shared vegetable plots. Neighbors chose together what they wanted to grow. It could give retired residents a project to work on together and help them get to know each other once they're no longer meeting people through work.
[05:59] LEO: Yes, activities are usually more enjoyable when they're shared. Do you think we could perhaps investigate?

passages.title: Music therapy for surgical patients
content: 📌 Music therapy for surgical patients
Background
After an operation, patients may experience discomfort or unwanted disruption to their [ _____ ].Most current recovery methods concentrate on controlling pain.
Recent research

An analysis brought together evidence from almost 100 [ _____ ] and found that music:improved patients’ reported wellbeing;enabled them to leave hospital sooner.Although individual preferences varied, the selected music generally had a [ _____ ] influence.Sound was usually delivered through music [ _____ ].Patients experienced hardly any [ _____ ].Hospital records showed that music listeners required a smaller amount of [ _____ ] than other patients.The greatest benefit occurred when patients were [ _____ ].Researchers believe music helped because it provided a [ _____ ].They advise offering either music or recordings from [ _____ ] to everyone having an operation.Further research will identify the ideal [ _____ ] setting.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: In part 4, you will hear part of a lecture for medical students about using music to support hospital patients having surgery. First, you have some time to look at questions 31-40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31-40. Today I'm going to discuss research into the use of music therapy for people who have an operation.

[00:57] AUDIO: Most of us will need some form of surgery during our lifetime. In the United States alone, over 51 million procedures are carried out each year. Recovery, however, is uncomfortable for a great many patients. Moving around may be difficult, and even raising themselves into a sitting position can seem exhausting.

[01:20] AUDIO: Their usual routine can be disrupted as well. They may be unable to do ordinary activities, for instance, or may have to spend a substantial amount of time attending physiotherapy sessions as part of their recovery. At present, post-operative care is largely centered on medication for pain control. Depending on how extensive the procedure was, this may be provided for a short period or for considerably longer.

[01:49] AUDIO: Yet music has not become a routine element of care after surgery, even though many studies indicate that it may aid recovery. Earlier this year, a team decided to bring together all the evidence available and show what music might contribute to surgical recovery. They found close to 100 trials, covering about 7,000 patients who had recorded music, included in their care after an operation. The team then examined the outcomes.

[02:22] AUDIO: Patients who heard music said they felt happier and more content during recovery. They also left hospitals sooner than comparable patients who received no music. Musical preferences differed widely across the group, so no single style dominated. What the selection shared was a calming effect.

[02:44] AUDIO: Some people used headphones. The sound was kept low enough for them to talk to nurses and other hospital staff. More commonly, however, the music came through specially designed pillows. These allow only the person resting on them to hear the audio.

[03:03] AUDIO: The music was tested at different stages before the operation while it was taking place afterwards or across more than one of these periods. Some patients listened once each day, whereas others had several listening sessions. When patients described how they had felt, they reported either no anxiety at all or only a small amount. By contrast, those who had not been given music expressed greater dissatisfaction.

[03:34] AUDIO: The researchers checked these personal reports against the patient's medical records. In every comparison, the music group needed less medication for pain than the group that did not listen. Neither the musical style nor the patient's choice made a substantial difference, and the timing before, during, or after the procedure was not especially important either. Music was beneficial even under a general anesthetic, although the effect was stronger when patients were awake.

[04:07] AUDIO: So the overall effect is positive, but the exact reason is still uncertain. In everyday life, people often use music to relax or take their minds off difficulties. The research team concluded that, for surgical patients, its main value came from distraction. It offered something familiar and gave patients a small area of control.

[04:34] AUDIO: The researchers now believe the evidence is strong enough for music to be offered to everyone undergoing surgery. Patients should be free to select what they hear. If they do not want music, recordings made in nature can be equally effective. Individual surgical teams may decide that patients should listen before the operation or immediately after returning to the ward.

[04:59] AUDIO: There are still questions to answer. The team's next study will determine the most suitable volume for the music, and I'm looking forward to seeing the findings. It will be interesting to discover whether… That is the end of part four.
[05:18] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
